review:
it's rough.
while advertised as an "open world survival craft", you're following a linear campaign story of fetch, kill, acquire, craft.
a lot of people call this is a Terraria-inspired game and I can see that.  The one thing I will point out in this is there is no water, no collapse of terrain and the game itself is a grid of smaller, generated zones, so there's an X,Y limit on every location.
There's really no point to building your own base apart from advancing levels in specific non-combat skills like farming and animal husbandry.
The enemy mobs and friendly summons have some really bad AI.
The majority of achievements are a time sink, with one in particular in the final hours of the story tied to completion of side quests requires finding specific books.  Up to this point, books do not serve any known purpose other than for lore in game. These books have a set spawn point and can disappear if you sell them. this required me to go into the save files to reset specific zones and loot them again.
The game really isn't difficult, its an unfun grind, every piece of equipment you craft is inferior to what you will loot and the drop rates vs progression means you're only smithing to gain more levels smithing.
the crafting system is based off of XP gain from what you craft and how much, relying entirely on recipes, there is no testing or experimentation in order to unlock, it's a roadmap.
There's a ton of really nice sprites in locations and biomes, majority of which you cannot interact with and are only for decoration, with some you can make for your base.
early game there are ridiculous platforming setups where you will be making multiple attempts to reach a "Secret" chest, these are tied to achievements and better/valuable gear, on more than one occasion I simply saved at a point and reloaded my attempts as it was quicker than navigating to the platform in-game.  this becomes a non-issue when you unlock double-jump, however it's at the end of a skill tree which is for non-combat attributes, which is locked based on character level in addition to following the tree, so it's only 7 skill unlocks but requires a minimum level just to move more freely in the game.
same issue with stamina, I don't mind there being a stamina bar in game, but one particular zone is a majority of fetch quests in a non-combat area, it's just padded runtime that has little reward expecting you to chase down NPCs.  You can raise stats to not consume stamina while running, but I only reached that point after the speedbump time-sink zones

One of the better crafting systems i've seen in a game with a huge tier ceiling of gear and a lot of loot unique to specific parts of the map.  

The way exploration works is you have a huge map with tiles. You select a tile on the map and each and every tile is its own level, making for an incredible amount of world to explore.

The tiles except for towns and dungeons are fully destroyable top to bottom and you can build anywhere except towns and dungeons so about 98% of the game is your open world to do whatever you want in.

I've done a small handful of quests and most gave me access to dungeons which are cool, all with their own secrets to hunt down which is a ton of fun and now i'm treating it more as a open ended adventure as a nameless adventurer and largely ignoring the story and quests because exploring and building my house and farm is satisfying.  

 I have almost all of the map unlocked, I'm raising too many chickens and pigs, and my garden takes 30 minutes to farm every rotation because there really is no limit to how big your base can be, it can even stretch across every map on every tile if you wanted it to which is massive.     Finding NPCs and bringing them home from the wild is pretty neat since it lets you build your own village basically.

I'd like to see more diverse mini biomes and area hazards like lava pools in the next game so you can't just dig straight down and have to put in more thought to navigating when digging but that aside, this is a load of fun.  The rain and thunderstorms are very atmospheric and fighting in them gives a nice immersive rush. 

If you like terraria or aground then give this a try, it has a lot of the same feel to it. They aren't the same games but those two and this game scratches a lot of the same itches that so few others even begin to scratch.

[h1] Une pépite ! [/h1]

[h2] Mon ressenti de cette expérience [/h2]
J'ai dévoré ce jeu et complété à 100% en une petite 50aines d'heures. Le tout sans me presser, sans try hard, et sans trop farm !

La courbe de progression est très fluide, dans mon cas, j'ai fait en sorte de réaliser toutes les quêtes secondaires et trouver tous les trésors de chaque acte avant d'entamer le suivant, j'imagine que les loots et l'expérience gagnés ont contribué à cette fluidité ! (Surtout les ennemis puissants qui dropent des orbes pour faire des parchemins de points de talent !)

[b]Le lore ou les stats sont très complètes.[/b]
» En tant qu'Elfe Noire, j'ai grandement apprécié le fait de savoir précisément quel est notre taux de régénération pour chaque barre (Vie, Mana, Stamina) en temps réel (Cf. l'affichage Character/General). Ce qui aide drastiquement afin d'élaborer un build optimisé.
» Le genre et la race, compte dans les dialogues, j'étais une Elfe Noire, et certains ne voulais pas me parler, car raciste ou misogyne, ça renforce drastiquement l'immersion.

[h2] Succès [/h2]
[b]Simple a réalisé[/b]
Une fois le boss final vaincu, j'étais niveau 44 (Personnage) et seulement 2 de mes métiers était niveau 100+, après 45 heures de jeu. Il m'a fallu 6h, pour obtenir tous mes métiers à 100%, mais surtout le niveau 50 !

[h3] Métiers Niveau 100 [/h3]
Je vous conseille de vous rendre auprès du spécialiste de chaque métier du plus haut niveau rencontré (en somme, allez voir le Forgeron de [i]StoneBridge[/i] et pas celui de [i]Woodbury[/i]), il vous proposera de vous entraîner pour maximum 19 Po / Niveau en fin de jeu.
Tips pour gagner beaucoup d'argent et rendre anecdotique l'achat des niveaux en fin de partie : [spoiler]Vendez vos [i]Greater Potions[/i] elles sont a 6 Po la potion et en fin de jeu, on en obtient beaucoup sur les zombies [/spoiler]

[h3] Personnage Niveau 50 [/h3]
J'ai farmé une 15aine de maps dans le dernier biome en nettoyant tout les mobs à la surface.
» Sachant que les mobs sous terre sont plus forts et délivrent plus d'expérience, j'ai d’abord opter pour ce choix, mais la difficulté de navigation dans les souterrains mène au fait que rester à la surface donne un meilleur ratio expérience/temps.
» Quand tous vos métier sont au niveau 100 et qu'ils ne vous reste plus que le niveau 50 à avoir ne perdez pas de temps à loot, vous gagnerez beaucoup [spoiler]BEAUCOUP[/spoiler] de temps !

[h2] Synthèse [/h2]
[h3] Points forts [/h3]
- Combat : Synergies des sorts et compétences
- Combat : Utiliser le clic gauche et droit en même temps !
- Narration : Les options dans les dialogues, même si des fois (je l'ai testé) certains choix mène à la même résolution, le voyage (en gros, les dialogues par lesquels on passe sont bien différents mais toujours cohérents)
- On n'a pas besoin de wiki !
Toutes les quêtes sont bien indiquées, sans pour autant avoir de grosses flèches rouges et être pris par la main.
Même les trésors, on nous indique le nombre obtenu par map, et généralement si on fouille ou parle à des PNJ, ils nous donnent des indices intradiégétiques au lore qui donne sens à l’emplacement des trésors rencontrés.
Néanmoins, si vous en souhaitez un, il y a celui-ci qui est top et peu aider si jamais on a passé un peu trop vite un dialogue :3
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2838920765

[h3] Point faible [/h3]
- La distance de détection des coffres autour de soi pour les crafts (Cela a eu pour conséquence dans mon gameplay de ne pas accorder a de crédits à la construction d'une base esthétique, car techniquement pas optimisé)

[h3] Conclusion [/h3]
- N'étant pas tellement adepte de ce genre de jeu, j'ai été très agréablement surpris d'y prendre autant plaisir !
- DONC FONCEZ ! D'autant plus s'il est en solde à moins de 6€ (comme pour moi)

Someone else described it as a cross between Terraria and the Elder Scrolls games (the earlier ones especially), and I'd say the comparison is pretty apt.

The open sections give you the freedom to dig / chop / build to your heart's content in a 2D world, like Terraria. The storied sections have you running around completing quests, chatting to NPCs, and generally killing with whatever arsenal of weapons and magic you feel like, much like the Elder Scrolls games.

Is it as good as either of them? No, of course not. Terraria has had many, many years to get to where it is today, and TES has all the resources of Bethesda.

RoM is the first game made by a small indie dev, and it shows. Both in the rough edges, and in the love that was poured in to making it. It is imperfect, but endearing nonetheless. Like Terraria was in the early days.

I definitely got my money's worth, and with a (free) remake version in the works, plus a sequel down the track, I look forward to coming back to the Realms of Magic in the future.

There's a good game here but it's got some amateur mistakes and design philosophy. First, the positives.

Artwork is fine mostly. It's a 2d survival crafting game. It's hard to screw this up. You have two hotbars you can switch between. One is for tools I think, which has an icon for using them. When you have a tool equipped, using this icon uses whatever tool for whatever material you're clicking automatically. so if you have both an axe and a shovel equipped, using the button/icon on a tree cuts it down with the axe and digging on the ground uses a shovel without you having to switch tools. The game takes place in a zelda 2 style map. You have the overworld map and chunks which you load into. I think it works well and takes me back to the nes/snes days.


This game also has rpg stats and level up mechanics. I love this stuff in crafting games but you rarely see it done properly if at all. I always have to rely on mods for this like Starbound with RPG Growth, but I'm glad it's just part of the core game here. it adds depth. Skills, weapons, farming. it's all here and it's done well for the most part. There's magic which supplements non-magic combat pretty well.

Hairs need to be redrawn and positioned properly.

Game is riddled with weird english. I get that it's not everyones' first language and I'm usually the last person to criticize grammar, but come on. it's just weird when I talk to someone, and they say stuff like 'One gold is pretty much, but I'll get it for you.' that makes no sense.

as far as I can tell, there are no sliders or variables you can change to alter your world, like enemy spawn rate or hunger depletion rate. It comes as it is. There appears to also be no modding support. Finally, gonna complain about this as I always do with survival sandbox games: why can we not claim land? I'm so tired of these games missing one important mechanic. Territory. Ingame currency -> buy plots of land -> invite people who are allowed permissions in this area -> taxes come out of residents' pockets and pay the upkeep -> expand with more money. This is an integral thing that kept a lot of Minecraft PVP servers and Terraria servers going back in the day. I rarely see this mechanic implemented even though it gives us something to do, a reason to care about building and defending. In games like this, NPCs could fill the role of the player residents. It's a amazing mechanic and, again, missing here unless I'm just not far enough along and it surprisingly is in this game.

7/10

I really can't help but compare this game to Terraria for good and ill.  It looks a lot like Terraria and has too many similar mechanics and activities for it to be a coincidence.  This is one of those games where I get the sense the devs played another game (in this case, Terraria) and got the idea in their head of how they'd have built it, instead.

The most obvious change is the existence of a plot/story.  This leads to a weird dichotomy in gameplay, because the "local map" you play on is relatively small, but you can open up a world map and go to different local maps by clicking on a grid location.  Most are procedurally-generated "sandbox" maps, which are basically just like Terraria where you can dig, explore, build your own house, etc.  Then, there are plot maps that are always the same, almost all the objects are fixed in place without you being able to dig or place any blocks and most furniture being non-interactive.  I find this quite jarring.  In particular, some areas in the plot maps, despite the game training you to stop trying to mine, you're meant to dig through special walls, (with "muck" blocks or the like, while the similar-looking mud blocks are still invincible.)  You're meant to find all the secrets in these plot areas, but since the game changes the rules on you depending on location, it's hard to remember all the tricks you're supposed to be using to search.

The plot is also... not fantastic.  It goes for a rather misanthropic "comedic" tone that leaves me not caring if I save or wind up dooming everyone.  It's like Monty Python's take on mud-stained illiterate peasants without the charm or flamboyance, and instead a general disdain for everyone.  The first town has a town idiot who steals women's clothing, introduces a guy as the local wife-beater whose violence everyone just ignores, and instead everyone warns you to stay away from the brutal authoritarian guard captain... who's also the only one with actual main plot quests.  As other reviews mention, there's little role-play here, as you only get choices during quest dialogue, and your options are effectively "agree to whatever they say," "agree but complain about it," or "refuse to do the quest." There's one main plot quest per chapter where you get A choice (basically "kill everyone" or "don't",) but otherwise, refusing either says "OK, I'll wait here until you agree" or "tough, do it anyway."

Another huge change is the RPG leveling system.  You have a race that gives bonuses, (or penalties for the gnome,) but the rest is based upon gear, finding scrolls (rewards for quests or in treasure chests in sandbox maps,) and spending talent points in one of seven talent trees.  There are a heavy and light weapon tree, a general mobility/recovery "combat" tree, and four magic trees: fire, ice, nature, and necromancy.  Because of how combat works, these have serious balance issues.

That brings me to the biggest change: Combat.  Unlike the NES-inspired Terraria, you can walk through enemies just fine, you only take damage if you're there when an enemy launches one of their heavily-choreographed attacks.  The combat is more like one of those "2d Soulslike" games where you right click to block and get a dodge roll where I-frames are second tier in the "combat' tree.  It seems designed to want you to dodgeroll, then stab the enemy in the back before waiting for the next attack and rolling again, although its stamina regeneration can be limiting.  Or you can just play a nature or necromancy mage and just drop summons on the enemy while hiding on a ledge like a total coward.  Even if you're a melee brute, you can easily just take a time out by jumping up on a ledge for a breather, as nearly all the enemies lack the scripting to understand how to jump more than a couple tiles up.  Your MP and HP regenerate, theirs doesn't.  It's like if going back to bonfires in Dark Souls didn't respawn enemies, you just clear them out once and they're gone forever.

This is both good and bad; Enemies in Terraria were often more [i]annoying[/i] than threatening.  I wound up just avoiding caves and tunneling blindly through the solid stone to pick up random metals I happened to bumble on rather than constantly fight unending streams of monsters while I'm trying to get some mining done.  Having the ability to just kill all the monsters in a given chamber and mine in peace means I'm not sick to death of the combat and actively seeking to avoid it.  On the other hand, no respawns mean clearing a map makes it [i]completely dead[/i] with no danger and nothing to do but continuously farm crops.  I find myself missing those periodic monster-spawning events like blood moons from Terraria so that there could be some peaks of action spacing out valleys of farming.

The maps are also gated by area.  This means that in the starting province, I dig down to see how far down the bottom of the map is, only to find that in those maps, once you hit a certain depth, content just [i]stops[/i].  You can only find tin, copper, salt, and coal in those maps, and if you go too deep, you just stop finding [i]anything[/i] but stone and dirt.  No lava or underworld at the bottom, the boundary is just boredom.

This results in a sort of forced pacing, because you can easily spin jute into burlap and gain weaving skills, which unlocks the ability to spin linen, but you don't get flax until the next province.  Meanwhile, you could focus on getting to the next province as fast as possible by just exploring sandbox maps for chests with map fragments (10 fragments to get to the next province, easily obtained in even a single sandbox map, of which dozens are in each province,) but when you get there, if you hadn't spent time farming jute and grinding weaving, you couldn't use the linen you found, anyway.  You're time-gated behind both, and neither has anything to do with the main plot and quests.  You're forced to split your time, which, if handled deftly might be a brilliant way to keep the game from getting too stale, but if there's one thing in this grab-bag of systems you don't like, it can repeatedly force you to do stuff like go mining for sandbox chests for map shards.

There are a lot of decorative items, and obviously, the devs loved setting up tons of detail in their hand-made plot maps, while seemingly all the stuff you see you can eventually build with enough skill ranks and materials.  The issue is, the game isn't built to let you have a home base - you can't carry rabbits from Splinterville back to your Woodsbury-area hut, so you need to build a new base in every province to get all the resources, and you can't mark a base with anything more than a tiny icon in the corner of a grid spot.  Also, because of the aforementioned lack of respawning enemies, raids where you defend your giant castle from assault like Terraria are right out.  It winds up making you feel like spending time actually [i]using[/i] the intricate decorations are a waste of effort since you never need them and will just be moving on, anyway.

Ultimately, I still find it interesting, with a clunkiness in combat and the relatively low amounts of combat being the weaker points of the game.  It's strong point, however, is the fusion blend of genres and the simple fact that I still just plain like this kind of freeform sandbox explorer/builder with a side of RPG build crafting.

Overall, it's an Indie dev "Terraria-like" with RPG leveling/profession mechanics and talent trees that boost select weapons or spells. Yes, it can be a bit grindy because of those RPG mechanics, but the grind doesn't feel too bad so far. Just don't rush quests only - do some mining trips & crafting, exploring areas for seeds and materials, and you'll get some extra kills in the process. 

It's an Indie dev game, so don't go in expecting AAA or something that has been receiving 10+years of updates & extra content like Terraria has gotten....

I want to like this game, but it has too many problems to ignore.

[olist]
[*]This isn't an RPG. Yes, it has things like hit points, a leveling system, skills, experience, etc. which a lot of people will equate with "RPG", but their own website talks up the story, and how Realms of Magic "IS a ROLEPLAYING game". Yet, your choices rarely matter, hell, there's a lot of lore about each race on the character creation screen, but everyone in the world reacts to you identically no matter what you choose, except the undead "Cursed" which could have been implemented as just a "attack literally everyone" mode. If I play a wood elf and approach a human settlement that's on the brink of war with a nearby wood elf settlement, and both sides treat me identically to the human character I made... so then how can you really claim that it's a "ROLEPLAYING" game? The story is...fine, pretty basic and predictable, but fine, but without any ability to really weave yourself into it and make meaningful choices that truly alter its outcomes it's not enough to carry the game. 

[*]This isn't an open world. Open world games are a pretty well defined concept at this point, and despite their own web page claiming it's an "Open world RPG", this isn't an open world game. Everything is sectioned off into instanced squares on a map grid, the map itself is segregated into wider zones which you can't access until you either complete the current zone's main quest line or kill enough random humanoid enemies to collect enough map fragments to craft a map which you use to unlock the next area. To be fair this system is fine, albeit a bit janky, but one thing it is absolutely not is an open world. 

[*]The combat isn't good enough to carry the game. It's just not. The weapon swings and movement often feel like you're in a pool of molasses or tar. No impact can be felt from weapon hits, except maybe the thrown knives, and everything is slow and floaty. Enemy AI is very basic, the movement system is basic (walk left/right, jump, sprint, dodge roll), no ledge grabbing, climbing, swimming (no open water anywhere), no synergy with weapon attacks and movement. There are no ranged weapons (you can select talents which grant you skills that can be used to perform a "throw dagger/axe" attack, but it behaves more like a magic spell attack), you cannot dual wield weapons, there are no two-handed weapons. The magic is mostly projectile attacks and "summon a creature who is a friendly NPC to attack enemies". There is no system for unarmed fighting.

[*]The art and visual style isn't good enough to carry the game. It's best described as "competent". Normally this would be fine, but compounded with the above issues it's just not good enough. My bigger problem with the art is that there are hand drawn stills on the loading screens that look nice, but it's clear that the pixel artist either didn't use them or barely used them as a reference. All the races are the same size. It's clear that the pixel artist made one body sprite, and then tweaked it a little bit for each race. But high elves (which are described as tall) are the same height as gnomes and goblins (which are described as the shortest). To try and make them more visually distinctive, the dwarves and gnomes are given goofy, puffy faces, but it's not always immediately obvious just by appearance. This ties into my comments in point 1 above. When all your different character types feel very samey it's hard to settle in to enjoy some actual role playing.

[*]The talent system has too much filler. Most of it is "X does Y% better" whether it's more damage, armor, health, or etc.. There are some good ideas, but it doesn't stand out among the rest of the game.

[*]The crafting system is fine, tho it's impossible to avoid comparing it to games like Terraria, which in that context, it feels slow and clunky.

[*]The building system lacks depth, quality of life features that contemporary games with the same system have had two years prior to the release of Realms of Magic. There are still bugs, which are minor, but add to the pile of issues above, and make complex builds a hassle rather that fun to execute.

[*]No controller support. For some, this is a preference, for others, this is an accessibility issue which can make games impossible to play without it. The developer has stated that there are no plans add this and that it'll be in "the Realms of Magic remake", speaking of...

[*]This game is "done", as in, there will be no more changes, improvements, bug fixes, etc. The dev got this game across the finish line and got their "Very Positive" Steam score. Do not buy this thinking it's a diamond in the rough, this diamond's as polished as it's ever going to get.
[/olist]

Overall it feels too unfocused. Reading the original Kickstarter page for this game, the devs had grand plans for player built cities, economic systems, 30 talent trees, and more, and it's very clear that they should have kept their ambitions more simple, as even in this pared down version of their original vision, the lack of focus and tightness of the game's systems shows. Its systems and components don't work together well enough or perform outstanding enough individually to make a good game, it's just a collection of things that are all okay or mediocre, and in this game market, with so many good titles to spend your money on I can't recommend buying this even on sale or spending your time on it.

Despite the game's title, playing a magic focused character is actually going to be very difficult at the start. You run out of mana after just a few spells and will have to retreat to a safe location while you wait for it to recharge. Additionally, cycling through spells is going to be rather tricky, as they're assigned to different numbers on the keyboard. My personal recommendation is to start off as a hybrid user of Magic and Weapons until you rank up a few levels where you can improve the effectiveness of your spells.

Another problem with the game is that without multiplayer, you'll find yourself having to dip your character into multiple different professions in order to advance yourself. At 45 Trading, the merchants you find around the place will have their full supplies unlocked, but this only covers up to Bronze level gear. If you want to make Iron or something grander, you're going to have to harvest and process the resources yourself. And if you want to even be able to do that, you'll need to grind up your profession level until the recipe becomes available.

This can result in your character feeling like they have no sense of identity. My first run, I wanted to be a goblin blacksmith, and ended up having to become a miner / farmer / woodcutter / leather worker / tailor / alchemist just so I'd have both the resources to do my desired job, and the funds needed to maintain them.

Speaking of funds, Alchemy is the best way to level up your Trading profession in the early game. Minor health / stamina / mana potions sell for 5 silver each, while Lesser Elixirs sell for 50. The resources needed to produce these are quite cheap and easy to come by even in the early game, so you can produce a ton of potions and sell them off for a decent profit.

Finally, I'll offer this word of advice for new players: AVOID BOARS!

Boars in this game are very tricky to deal with as they keep doing 'hit and run' tactics to charge through you and your summons. But worse than that, once they detect your presence, they will not stop following you across the entire map, no matter how far or how fast you run. The only way to get them off your tail is to dig one block wide straight down into the ground where the boar can not follow you and then tunnel your way to safety while it's stuck at the entrance.
